Nyaya Sutra 1.1.3 (the four means of knowing)

roots.context: We have run fair tests, kept a control and written our results in tables. Now we ask what fair tests tell us about how we know anything.

deep_truth.truth: Your lemon slice stayed white, but on its own that proved nothing. It meant something only beside the plain slice, which browned in the same air. A cause can be seen only by comparing. To know what one thing does, you must also watch what happens without it.
deep_truth.habit: We think we can see a cause just by watching it work: lemon goes on, the slice stays white. But the white slice alone could not tell us whether it would have stayed white anyway. Only the comparison with the plain slice showed what the lemon did.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Brown Apple Test, the plain slice and the lemon slice came from one apple, sat on one plate and waited the same time. Only the lemon was different, and only by putting the two side by side could you see what the lemon did.

three.who_am_i: You know you have grown only by comparing: a pencil mark on the wall from last year.
three.what_is_life: A cut apple browns because the plant's cells answer the cut. Living things are always answering what happens to them.
three.what_is_this_world: Air, warmth and the cut were acting on every slice at once. In the world, many causes always act together.

roots.thread: On the plate, air, warmth, the cut and the apple's own substances all act together on each slice. Nature does them all at once, as one happening. In a fair test, we hold all but one of them the same, so that one can be noticed. The many causes we name are parts we pick out of one whole happening. Science studies the parts, and the parts still belong to one whole.

teachings.teaching: The Buddha told the Kalama people not to accept a teaching only because it is old, often repeated, written in a book, or said by a respected teacher. When you know for yourselves that something is true and good, then accept it.
teachings.link: The navy's doctors trusted acids to cure scurvy because respected people said so. James Lind tested the cures side by side and saw for himself which one worked.

teachings.teaching: The Nyaya school names four ways of knowing: perception (seeing for yourself), inference (working out from what you saw), comparison, and the word of a trustworthy person.
teachings.link: A fair test uses the first three together. You perceive the white and brown slices, you compare them, and you infer that the lemon made the difference.

science.text: Doctors test new medicines in controlled trials: one group gets the medicine, a similar group does not, and chance decides who goes where.
Some things, like stars or the Earth's past, cannot be changed on purpose. Scientists compare many careful observations instead.

other_view.who: The Charvaka school of ancient India
other_view.view: The Charvakas said that only what we perceive directly is sure knowledge. Inference can always be wrong, because we can never check every case. You saw a white slice and a brown slice. Saying 'the lemon caused it' is an inference, and a new apple might behave differently.

practice.title: One thing different
practice.say: Let's sit still and close our eyes. Listen to all the sounds around us for a few breaths. Now I will change just one thing. I will open the window, or switch off the fan. Keep listening. What is different now? Only one thing changed, so you can hear exactly what it did. Open your eyes slowly.
practice.kid: Sit still. Close your eyes. Listen to every sound. The grown-up changes one thing. Listen again. What is different now?

ask: If you can only see a cause by comparing, can you ever see the cause of something that has happened only once?
Can anything in the world be kept exactly the same, even for a minute?
When you learn something about yourself, what are you comparing it with?

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home, with the materials listed. Apple slices: the plain slice usually shows browning at the edges within 10 to 20 minutes in a warm room, and is clearly brown by 30 minutes to an hour. Some apples brown slowly, so the steps say to check again at 30 minutes and 1 hour, and to play a game while waiting. Lemon juice keeps the slice white or nearly white for an hour or more. A quick dip in plain water changes little once the slice is back in the air. Salt water usually slows browning a little. Brinjal floats, so the Brinjal Bowl test holds each piece under with a small katori, otherwise its top browns in the air and the test is unfair. Cut brinjal browns within minutes, so 20 minutes is enough. Ten Throws works in any room with a bucket and a newspaper ball, and results differ from child to child. The sugar puzzle uses warm tap or flask water, not hot. The James Lind act-out uses paper slips only. The spine (intro, The Unfair Bounce, the Brown Apple Test, explanations, roots and quiz) fits about 85 minutes, with the apple's waiting time filled by the cards and the Fair or Unfair? game.

how_we_found_out.story: For hundreds of years, sailors on long voyages fell ill with scurvy. Their gums bled, their teeth came loose, and many died. Doctors had many ideas about the cure. A popular one in the British navy was 'elixir of vitriol', a weak acid. On 20 May 1747, James Lind, a doctor on the ship HMS Salisbury, did something new. He took twelve sailors with scurvy who were as alike as he could find. They slept in the same part of the ship and ate the same food. He split them into six pairs and gave each pair a different treatment: cider, elixir of vitriol, vinegar, sea water, a paste of garlic, mustard and other spices, or two oranges and a lemon each day. After six days, one sailor from the oranges and lemons pair was fit for work again, and the other was much better. The pair with cider improved a little. The acid, the vinegar and the sea water did not help. Lind published his results in 1753. Even so, it took the navy until 1795 to give sailors lemon juice. We now know that scurvy comes from too little vitamin C.
how_we_found_out.who: James Lind, a Scottish ship's doctor in the British navy
how_we_found_out.when: 20 May 1747 (the test on HMS Salisbury), 1753 (his book A Treatise of the Scurvy)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many doctors thought acids such as elixir of vitriol or vinegar cured scurvy. Lind's fair test, with the same food and quarters for every pair, showed that these did not help, while oranges and lemons did.
